header.scope: Lost: international traffic moved to local acquiring; the US business stayed with us.
header.tag_why: Stefan compared approval performance by country, card type and issuer against Adyen's real-traffic test results, and we answered with an average uplift instead of his own numbers until after the test had finished.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For payments leaders reviewing performance by market, replace the average-uplift claim with an offer built on their own traffic: 'Your approvals in every market: where you're declining, why, and what we'd fix.' Use 'approvals', not 'authorization rates'. Name the cost the way the customer did ('Money left on the table'). Make the deliverable something they can take to their CFO: their own approval rates by market, with the money attached.
messaging_changes.why: Stefan rejected the average-uplift deck with 'that's an average. What's mine?' and said 'I can't take an average to my CFO', while the analysis of his own data was the most useful thing we sent him.

messaging_changes.change: When a buyer raises 'local acquiring' or 'Local cards, local rails', do not argue the mechanism. Offer a fast readout on their own international traffic: approval rate by country, card type and issuer, with the reason for each decline. Deliver it before any competitor test finishes. Suggested line: 'Before you decide, let's look at your approvals country by country, card by card, issuer by issuer, and why.'
messaging_changes.why: Adyen won by testing the customer's own international traffic and reporting results by country, card type and issuer. Our equivalent analysis arrived three weeks after Stefan asked, when the test had already finished.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For accounts with a dedicated payments owner, add a named person to the support story alongside the response-time tiers: 'A named person at Stripe reviews your approvals by market with you every month.' Use this only once a recurring, named review actually exists for that kind of account.
messaging_changes.why: Stefan asked 'who at Stripe looks at his numbers every month' and the rep had no name. He also said 'I heard from Stripe when I said I was leaving'. Response-time tiers did not answer that question.

trigger.insight: No product problem was reported before the evaluation started. It started because a new owner applied a lens we had never shown this account: declines by country. Our champion left last year and we never noticed the replacement, so the account looked 'healthy' only because nobody was measuring what Stefan measured. Our global positioning lost exactly in the international markets, Brazil and 'a couple in Europe', and we still don't know which European markets or what his numbers showed.
trigger.messaging: Back M1's 'grow globally, in every currency' with a proactive per-market approval readout, delivered whenever a new payments owner appears, so the first decline pull a new leader runs is one we already ran with them.

decider.insight: The real audience was a CFO we only hear about through Stefan. The transcript doesn't establish that we ever spoke to the CFO. We learned the recommendation had already gone up only on our last call, so the decision moved past us without our knowledge. Stefan told us the format the CFO needed: his company's own figures, not a benchmark. That is the clearest buying-criteria signal in the whole review.
decider.messaging: Build the acceptance story as a CFO-ready artifact with the customer's own approvals by market and the money attached, not a deck of averages a champion can't forward.

competitor.insight: Adyen didn't win on a claim. It won on a test against the customer's own traffic, which reset Stefan's standard of proof to country, card type and issuer, with a reason for each. We don't know what the test showed, so any belief that Adyen's approvals were better is unverified. What we do know is that their format beat our format. 'Local acquiring' became Stefan's frame, and the rep says she had no counter to it.
competitor.messaging: When a buyer says 'local acquiring', answer with an offer to measure their own international traffic by country and issuer within days, and equip reps with a tested response to the local-acquiring argument.

message.insight: The rep says 'we weren't really pitching', but we did pitch M4 and it was rejected outright. The roadmap offer was declined too. The only thing that landed was the custom analysis of his own data, which shows the content was right and the timing and format were wrong. The developer and billing goodwill the rep credits for keeping the US is her own read, not something Stefan said.
message.messaging: Replace M4's average-uplift claim with 'here are your approvals by market and what we'd fix', and make the payments-performance analysis the default renewal motion instead of a rescue.

decided.insight: The rep's view that nothing could be done conflicts with her own account. Stefan asked for exactly what we eventually delivered and called it our most useful work, but it arrived three weeks later, after Adyen's test was done. The turning point looks like that three-week gap, not some decision made before we arrived. It is unclear whether our analysis reached him before or after the recommendation went to the CFO.
decided.messaging: Make per-market approval analysis a same-week response to any decline-by-country question, because in a head-to-head test the first credible answer on the customer's own data sets the frame.

gaps.insight: Both gaps are about service, not features. We could produce the analysis but not on demand, and we had no named person watching his numbers each month. M5 sells tiered response times, which answers how fast do you reply to a ticket. Stefan asked who is watching me. His line about hearing from us only when he said he was leaving shows how our coverage looked to him.
gaps.messaging: Add a named, recurring owner of the customer's approval performance (a monthly review with a person's name on it) to the support story alongside M5's response-time tiers.

language.insight: Stefan describes a revenue leak in his own markets ('money left on the table', 'what's mine'). We describe a product feature ('Authorization Boost', 'Adaptive Acceptance') in vocabulary he doesn't use. 'Local cards, local rails' is a mechanism he can picture, while machine-learning uplift is a mechanism he has to trust. The competitor's language matched his mental model and ours didn't.
language.messaging: Rewrite M4 in buyer language, roughly: see the approvals you're losing in each market and the money behind them, using 'approvals' rather than 'authorization rates'.

gaps.follow_up: Have Elena ask Stefan, now that the decision is made, what the country-level results were and which number convinced the CFO.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got a reaction, and which got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena what Stefan said, in his words, when he received the payments-performance analysis, and whether anything besides that analysis drew interest.

gaps.question: When did you first feel this was lost? What happened right before?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena to put dates on the split request, Stefan's analysis request, Adyen's test ending, our analysis landing and the CFO approval, to see whether our analysis arrived before the recommendation went up.

gaps.question: Did anyone from our side ever meet the CFO?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena whether we had any contact with the CFO, and whether our analysis reached the CFO.

gaps.question: Was the international business confirmed to Adyen, or to another local acquirer?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena to confirm with Stefan who now processes the international traffic.

close.rep_takeaway: A healthy account with no tickets can still be at risk. When the person who bought us leaves, treat the account as open: find the new owner, run their numbers by market before they do, and put a name on who watches them every month. Here our analysis was the most useful thing we sent, but it arrived three weeks late, and that delay cost us more than any gap in the pitch.
